title: SYSK Selects: Who Gets to Name Continents?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on who gets to name continents (original episode aired on March 16). The hosts trace the supercontinent Pangaea and its ocean Panthalassa, Alfred Wegener's continental drift theory and supporting evidence (coal deposits, fossils, matching mountain ranges), and the breakup into Laurentia, Gondwana, Laurasia and the modern continents. They discuss what counts as a true continent, then the naming histories: Antarctica (John Murray, 1904, opposite of Arctic), America (Amerigo Vespucci controversy, Waldseemüller's 1507 map, possible Mayan or Nicaraguan origin of the word, Richard Amerik and John Cabot theory), Australia (Matthew Flinders vs. Terra Australis and Hieronymus Surian's earlier map), and Africa, Asia and Europe (likely named by sailors, with Phoenician and other theories). Also covers how some cultures count only North America, South America and Eurasia as continents. Includes off-topic movie banter and a listener mail about a road trip.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: The hosts open with a teaser about who names continents, chat about maps and food, and a preview of the geography topic.

segments.title: Pangaea and continental drift
segments.summary: The hosts describe the supercontinent Pangaea surrounded by the ocean Panthalassa, and Alfred Wegener's 1915 continental drift theory with evidence from coal deposits, fossils and matching mountain ranges.

segments.title: Breakup of supercontinents
segments.summary: The breakup of Pangaea into Laurentia, Gondwana and Laurasia, the later splits, the climate of the interior, and ongoing plate movement such as Australia moving toward Asia.

segments.title: What counts as a continent
segments.summary: The hosts define a true continent as a landmass surrounded by ocean and discuss how Europe, Asia and Russia blur the boundaries, and how some cultures recognize fewer continents.

segments.title: Naming Antarctica
segments.summary: John Murray and the HMS Challenger expedition came close to Antarctica, and in 1904 he named it as a combination of anti and Arctic, meaning opposite the North Pole.

segments.title: Origin of the name America
segments.summary: The Amerigo Vespucci controversy, Columbus's mistaken belief, Waldseemüller's 1507 map being the first to use America, the name-change claim, and theories that the name came from a Mayan or Nicaraguan word or from John Cabot's backer Richard Amerik.

segments.title: Break and movie sidebar
segments.summary: Break and off-topic movie chat about Gene Hackman, Robin Williams, Couch Trip and John C. Reilly, plus casting ideas for a P.T. Barnum film.

segments.title: Naming Australia
segments.summary: Matthew Flinders is credited with the name Australia over Terra Australis, but an 1855 map by Hieronymus Suriaco Jakob Sumbarth may have labeled it Australia earlier.

segments.title: Naming Africa, Asia and Europe
segments.summary: No documentation exists for these names; likely named by seafaring people. Theories include the Afri people, Latin for sunny, Phoenician sunrise and sunset words, and the mythological Europa.

segments.title: Continents in different parts of the world
segments.summary: Some parts of the world recognize only North America, South America and Eurasia as continents, and the hosts close the topic with a joke about the pavement T-shirt.

segments.title: Listener mail: road tripping
segments.summary: A listener couple on a road trip from Texas to Florida say they became hooked on the podcast on the drive.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to social media, email and the website.
